introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Physics 2 (0780), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2023. Time allowed: three hours.**

Answer ALL questions. Section I is designed to be answered in 1 hour, Section II in 30 minutes and Section III in 1 hour. You are advised to divide your time accordingly. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. In calculations you must show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. Calculators and formulae booklet are allowed.

**Structure of the paper.** SECTION I (headed "One hour 30 minutes" on page 2): questions 1 to 5 are compulsory; in question 6 answer EITHER 6 (a), (b) and (c) OR 6 (d), (e) and (f). SECTION II (40 minutes): DATA ANALYSIS, question 7. SECTION III (50 minutes): OPTIONS - answer any two questions from the four options (Option 1: Energy resources and environmental physics, question 8; Option 2: Communication, question 9; Option 3: Electronics, question 10; Option 4: Medical physics, question 11).

No data sheet is printed in the paper: whenever a constant is needed, the model answer states the value it uses.

questions.enonce_markdown:
**EITHER 6 (a), (b) and (c)**

(i) Define the temperature coefficient of resistance of a material. *[4 marks]*

(ii) State and explain the type of temperature coefficient of resistance copper has ie whether it is positive or negative. *[4 marks]*

(iii) Describe an experiment to measure the temperature coefficient of resistance of copper. Your description should include a setup, measurements taken, how the measurements are processed to reach a conclusion and at least one precaution. *[8 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) The **temperature coefficient of resistance** $\alpha$ of a material is the fractional change in its resistance, relative to its resistance at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, per unit rise in temperature:

$$\alpha = \frac{R_\theta - R_0}{R_0\,\theta}$$

where $R_0$ is the resistance at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $R_\theta$ the resistance at $\theta\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Its unit is $\mathrm{K^{-1}}$ (or $^\circ\mathrm{C}^{-1}$). Equivalently $R_\theta = R_0(1 + \alpha\theta)$.

(ii) For copper, $\alpha$ is **positive**: the resistance of copper increases as its temperature rises.

Explanation: copper is a metal, with a fixed number of free (conduction) electrons per unit volume that does not change appreciably with temperature. When the temperature rises, the positive ions of the lattice vibrate with larger amplitude, so the conduction electrons collide with them more often. The mean time between collisions falls, so the drift velocity for a given p.d. (and hence the current) falls, and the resistance $R = \rho L/A$ rises, because the resistivity $\rho$ increases. (In a semiconductor, in contrast, the number of charge carriers increases rapidly with temperature, so $\alpha$ is negative.)

(iii) **Apparatus:** a coil of insulated (enamelled) copper wire of a few ohms; a boiling tube containing oil with the coil immersed in it; a beaker of water to act as a water bath, with a Bunsen burner (or electric heater), tripod and gauze; ice; a thermometer ($-10$ to $110\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$); a stirrer; a digital ohmmeter (or a low-voltage cell, rheostat, ammeter and voltmeter); connecting leads.

**Set-up (diagram described):** the coil lies in the oil in the boiling tube, which stands in the water bath; the thermometer bulb is level with the coil; the two ends of the coil go out of the tube to the ohmmeter (or the ammeter in series and the voltmeter across the coil).

**Measurements:** 1. With the bath at melting ice ($0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$), stir, wait until the thermometer reading is steady, and read the resistance $R$ of the coil (with the ammeter and voltmeter, $R = V/I$). 2. Heat the bath slowly; at each rise of about $10\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ (up to about $90\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$) remove the flame, stir the water and oil, wait for the steady state, then read the temperature $\theta$ and the resistance $R$. 3. Record the readings in a table of $\theta/^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and $R/\Omega$.

**Processing:** since $R = R_0 + R_0\alpha\theta$, plot a graph of $R$ (vertical axis) against $\theta$. The points lie on a straight line: the **gradient** is $R_0\alpha$ and the **intercept** on the $R$ axis is $R_0$. Then
$$\alpha = \frac{\text{gradient}}{\text{intercept}}.$$

**Conclusion:** $R$ increases linearly with $\theta$ (positive gradient), so copper has a positive temperature coefficient of resistance, and the value of $\alpha$ obtained is of the order of $4\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}$.

**Precautions:** keep the current small and switch it off between readings, so that the heating of the wire by the current does not raise its temperature above that of the bath; stir well and wait for thermal equilibrium so the thermometer reads the temperature of the coil; keep the thermometer bulb next to the coil and read it at eye level to avoid parallax; use an oil bath so that the wire is insulated from water; allow for or subtract the resistance of the leads.

questions.enonce_markdown:
A $12.0\ \mathrm{V}$ steady power supply of negligible internal resistance, energizes a circuit comprising 4 resistors, as show in figure 3.

![fig-1](gce-al-physics-2023-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_6_fig_1.png)

When the switch is closed, calculate:

(i) the combined resistance of the circuit;

(ii) the change in the current in the circuit when the $4.00\ \Omega$ resistor is disconnected. *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
The $6.00\ \Omega$ resistor is in series with the parallel combination of $R_2 = 2.00\ \Omega$, $R_3 = 4.00\ \Omega$ and $R_4 = 2.00\ \Omega$.

(i) Parallel part:
$$\frac{1}{R_p} = \frac{1}{2.00} + \frac{1}{4.00} + \frac{1}{2.00} = 1.25\ \Omega^{-1} \Rightarrow R_p = 0.800\ \Omega$$

$$R_{\mathrm{total}} = 6.00 + 0.800 = 6.80\ \Omega$$

**Combined resistance $= 6.80\ \Omega$.**

(ii) Current with all resistors: $I_1 = \dfrac{12.0}{6.80} = 1.765\ \mathrm{A}$.

With the $4.00\ \Omega$ resistor disconnected, $R_2$ and $R_4$ remain in parallel:
$$R_p' = \frac{2.00\times2.00}{2.00+2.00} = 1.00\ \Omega,\qquad R_{\mathrm{total}}' = 6.00 + 1.00 = 7.00\ \Omega$$

$$I_2 = \frac{12.0}{7.00} = 1.714\ \mathrm{A}$$

$$\Delta I = I_2 - I_1 = 1.714 - 1.765 = -0.0504\ \mathrm{A}$$

**The current decreases by about $0.050\ \mathrm{A}$ (from $1.76\ \mathrm{A}$ to $1.71\ \mathrm{A}$).**

questions.enonce_markdown:
A Physics student in a village that is not electrified uses a $12.0\ \mathrm{V}$ motorcycle battery charge his mobile phone battery of emf $4.6\ \mathrm{V}$. He connects two filament bulbs in series with the phone battery to ensure that the high voltage does not destroy his phone battery.

(i) If the charging current in the circuit is $0.8\ \mathrm{A}$, determine the resistance of each filament bulb.

(ii) Explain why the bulbs go off when the phone battery is fully charged. *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) The phone battery opposes the charging current, so the net p.d. driving the current through the two bulbs in series is
$$V_{\mathrm{net}} = 12.0 - 4.6 = 7.4\ \mathrm{V}.$$

Total resistance of the two bulbs (internal resistances neglected):
$$R_{\mathrm{total}} = \frac{V_{\mathrm{net}}}{I} = \frac{7.4}{0.8} = 9.25\ \Omega.$$

Assuming the two bulbs are identical, each has resistance
$$R = \frac{9.25}{2} = 4.6\ \Omega\ (4.63\ \Omega).$$

(ii) As the phone battery charges, the p.d. it opposes to the charger rises, so the net p.d. $12.0\ \mathrm{V} - V_{\mathrm{battery}}$ available to drive current through the bulbs falls, and the charging current falls. When the battery is full it can accept no more charge, so the net p.d. and the current drop to (nearly) zero. The power dissipated in each filament, $P = I^2R$, then falls to (almost) zero, the filaments cool and stop glowing: **the bulbs go off, which shows that charging is complete.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
**OR 6 (d), (e) and (f)**

(i) Define uniform acceleration.

(ii) State and explain a situation where an object in uniform motion is accelerating. *[4 marks for (i) and (ii) together]*

(iii) Describe an experiment to measure the acceleration of free fall of an object close to the earth's surface. Your description should include a setup, measurements taken, how the measurements are processed to reach a conclusion and at least one precaution that when taken improves the results. *[8 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) **Uniform acceleration** is motion in which the velocity changes at a constant rate, that is, by equal amounts in equal intervals of time, in a fixed direction: $a = \dfrac{\Delta v}{\Delta t} = \text{constant}$.

(ii) A body moving **at constant speed in a circle** (for example a car going round a roundabout at constant speed, or a satellite in circular orbit). Its speed is constant, but acceleration is the rate of change of **velocity**, a vector. The direction of the velocity changes continuously, so the velocity changes and the body accelerates, with an acceleration $a = v^2/r$ directed towards the centre of the circle, which needs a resultant force (centripetal force) in that direction.

(iii) **Apparatus:** a steel ball bearing, an electromagnet with a switch, a trap-door (or contact plate) switch, an electronic timer (millisecond), a retort stand, a metre rule, a plumb line.

**Set-up (diagram described):** the electromagnet is clamped at the top of a vertical stand holding the ball. The trap-door switch lies directly below, on the base. Releasing the ball with the switch starts the timer; the ball hits the trap-door, which stops the timer. The height $h$ from the bottom of the ball to the trap-door is measured with the metre rule.

**Measurements:** for about six values of $h$ (for example $0.30, 0.50, 0.70, 0.90, 1.10, 1.30\ \mathrm{m}$) release the ball, record the fall time $t$ and repeat three times at each height to take the mean $t$. Tabulate $h$, $t$ and $t^2$.

**Processing:** the ball starts from rest, so $h = \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$. Plot $h$ (vertical axis) against $t^2$. The graph is a straight line through the origin, with gradient $\tfrac{1}{2}g$, so
$$g = 2\times\text{gradient}.$$

**Conclusion:** the straight line through the origin shows that $h \propto t^2$, which confirms constant acceleration; $g$ comes out near $9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

**Precautions (any one improves the results):** use a small, dense steel ball so that air resistance is negligible; repeat each timing and take the mean; use a large range of heights so that timing errors are a small fraction of $t$; place a thin non-magnetic sheet (paper) on the electromagnet so that residual magnetism does not delay the release; check the rule is vertical and read at eye level.

Take $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. The ball is treated as a body sliding without friction (the question gives negligible friction), starting from rest.

(i) The component of the weight along the ramp gives the acceleration:
$$a = g\sin\theta = 9.8\times\sin30.0^\circ = 4.90\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}.$$

(ii) From $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$ with $u = 0$ and $s = 8.00\ \mathrm{m}$:
$$t = \sqrt{\frac{2s}{a}} = \sqrt{\frac{2\times8.00}{4.90}} = 1.81\ \mathrm{s}.$$

(iii) Speed at the base of the ramp: $v = \sqrt{2as} = \sqrt{2\times4.90\times8.00} = 8.85\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

Kinetic energy at the base: $E_k = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}\times0.500\times8.85^2 = 19.6\ \mathrm{J}$ (check: $mgh = 0.500\times9.8\times8.00\sin30.0^\circ = 19.6\ \mathrm{J}$).

On the floor the constant friction force $F$ does work $F\times d$ to remove this energy over $d = 15.0\ \mathrm{m}$:
$$F\,d = E_k \Rightarrow F = \frac{19.6}{15.0} = 1.31\ \mathrm{N}.$$

**Friction force $\approx 1.31\ \mathrm{N}$** (deceleration $2.61\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$). Assumptions: horizontal floor, constant friction, no loss of speed where the ramp meets the floor.

questions.enonce_markdown:
A football player takes a spot kick $40.0\ \mathrm{m}$ from a $2.2\ \mathrm{m}$ high empty goal post during training. If she kicks the ball with a velocity of $40.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ at an angle of $10.0^\circ$ to the ground:

(i) show by calculation whether she hits the target; and

(ii) explain why the path of the ball is parabolic. *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Take $g = 9.8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ and neglect air resistance.

(i) Components of the initial velocity:
$$u_x = 40.0\cos10.0^\circ = 39.4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}},\qquad u_y = 40.0\sin10.0^\circ = 6.95\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$$

Time to travel $40.0\ \mathrm{m}$ horizontally:
$$t = \frac{40.0}{39.4} = 1.015\ \mathrm{s}$$

Height of the ball at that time:
$$y = u_yt - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2 = 6.95\times1.015 - 4.9\times(1.015)^2 = 7.05 - 5.05 = 2.00\ \mathrm{m}$$

The ball is $2.00\ \mathrm{m}$ above the ground when it reaches the goal line, which is **below** the $2.2\ \mathrm{m}$ height of the goal post (crossbar), and above the ground (it is falling, with $v_y = 6.95 - 9.8\times1.015 = -3.0\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$). **So the ball goes into the goal: she hits the target.**

(ii) Horizontally no force acts on the ball (air resistance neglected), so the horizontal velocity is constant: $x = (u\cos\theta)t$. Vertically the only force is the weight, giving a constant downward acceleration $g$: $y = (u\sin\theta)t - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$. Eliminating $t$:
$$y = x\tan\theta - \frac{g\,x^2}{2u^2\cos^2\theta},$$
which is a quadratic in $x$ ($y = ax - bx^2$), the equation of a **parabola**.
